Every week a new large language model (LLM) is released, and with it comes a battery of numbers to prove its incremental improvement over existing models. These numbers come from "benchmarks" -- a series of evaluations that domain experts carefully create. Recently, two very different companies released bioinformatics-specific benchmarks: Genentech[^genentech], one of the oldest and most successful pharma companies, and Anthropic[^anthropic], a top AI company. The two companies couldn't be more different, and I think it shows in their benchmarks.

In this post I looked at some of the questions and evaluations in these benchmarks and share some thoughts about the quality, relevance, and why I think these results show that I'm not going to replaced by AI anytime soon. 

[^genentech]: Genentech, a 50-year-old pharma company with dozens of approved drugs and hundreds of clinical trials, released [CompBioBench](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.64898/2026.04.06.716850v1) [@compbiobench] on April 4th, 2026. The reputation of the authors' affiliations sets an expectation on their dataset. This is a benchmark created by some of the most experienced practitioners in the industry.

[^anthropic]: [BioMysteryBench](https://www.anthropic.com/research/Evaluating-Claude-For-Bioinformatics-With-BioMysteryBench) [@biomysterybench] was created by Anthropic, possibly one of the most important companies in the world right now. They are known for producing the world's leading LLM models. Their investments in life sciences research are highly intriguing. We will see what the pay off (if any) will be - we are still in early days.

# Anthropic and Genentech's benchmarking philosophy

There are many [ways to design LLM benchmarks](https://cameronrwolfe.substack.com/p/llm-bench). Previous bioinformatics benchmarks like [BixBench](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.00096) evaluate LLM performance whether conclusions match up with scientists'. But in science, often there are multiple reasonable approaches to a question, that might end up leading to differing but reasonable conclusions. Other benchmarks like scBench are fairly prescriptive in the series of "steps" that a model must take to complete a task, but that hampers creativity which is a core tenant of innovative scientific research.

It's both notable and validating that Anthropic and Genentech, independently and concurrently, decided on the same strategy for model evaluation. Both benchmarks are designed such that there is a single data-verifiable ground truth answer, and evaluations are non-prescriptive in how to arrive at that answer. Multiple paths are not necessarily encouraged, but models are free to "wander" different paths to reach their conclusions.

For example, both benchmarks have many questions classified as "metadata retrieval". These types of questions involve presenting some data (transcriptomic, epigenetic, etc.) to the model and asking questions about the sample identity: *are these samples male/female? what tissue is this scRNAseq sample from?*. These are good questions because they are data verifiable - the identity of the sample is known but kept hidden from the model, and they are relevant; they require leveraging biological and technological knowledge, and can require interaction with additional datasets to reach the answer (e.g. mapping transcripts identifiers to genes using a public database).

Another type of question that CompBioBench uses is synthetic and data augmentation. For example genomic content from contaminant species can be added to an existing dataset, and then the model is tasked with identifying the contaminant species. These are also "data-verifiable", and have the added benefit that only the authors know the answer to the question. In metadata retrieval, where samples are often pulled from published datasets, models have a small possibility of "cheating" - for example by finding the answer through matching to the paper itself, circumventing any usage of bioinformatics in it's solution. 

The last notable difference is how the answer is scored. CompBioBench uses an "exact string match" of the agent's answer and the ground truth, so the tasks are very explicit about the answer format, with some tolerance for numerical answers. BioMysteryBench, on the other hand, uses an LLM-as-a-judge.

I initially thought a deterministic evaluation was clearly the better approach. But after researching LLM-as-as-judge approach, I learned: it's very common, there are advantages and disadvantages[^llm-as-a-judge]; and ultimately I'm unsure if one approach is significantly better than the other. 

[^llm-as-a-judge]: One advantage of LLM-as-a-judge approach is that due to model reasoning capabilities, LLMs can catch "cheating". An example of cheating in bioinformatics might be if a model chooses to solve the task, not by using a bioinformatics approach, like comparing classifying a transcriptomic profile against known gene signatures, but instead by finding the answer through some shortcut, like matching a sample's identity to a published database or article [@gu2024survey].

# How rigorously these benchmarks are documented

It's worth first discussing the difference in how these two teams chose to publish their results.

Genentech published their benchmark on bioRxiv, which is a popular preprint server in the bioinformatics field. Their benchmark, problem statement, and results are presented in standard scientific article format. This means everything is deeply documented. And the article itself is hosted by bioRxiv, meaning a non-affiliated organization is ensuring the original content stays accessible[^journal-vs-blog].

[^journal-vs-blog]: And unlike a blog, which can be taken down or edited without any trace of original content, a preprint server is managed by a third party organization (bioRxiv is managed by Cold Spring Harbour), which includes keeping the original published article accessible and has a system for managing updates.

In contrast, Anthropic announced BioMysteryBench with a blog post. As you can imagine, the difference between a published article and blog post is vast. There is no standard format for a blog post like there is for a journal article. There is no in depth section describing how the questions were developed, there are no supplementary figures, and in general it is really hard to dig into details.

The Genentech team, I imagine is likely preparing the article for submission at a peer-reviewed journal. This means transparency is not optional; it's required and enforced to some degree by the journal and the peer reviews. They must describe their methods fully; they must defend their decisions, and they must be comprehensive in their scope as reasonably possible; some journals even enforce reproducibility and open source code[^cbb-github]. CompBioBench showed that all top models performed similarly, including Anthropics but also GPT from OpenAi, and Gemini from Google (might I mention, similar performance at a much lower cost!). Anthropic chose only to evaluate and publish only their own models.

[^cbb-github]: Genentech published a github repo that hosts the code to fully reproduce their results for CompBioBench: [Genentech/compbiobench-runner](https://github.com/Genentech/compbiobench-runner), which is amazing exemplar for transparency and reproducibility. This type of practice is a big step in building trust in their results. 

# Coverage over bioinformatics subdomains

Bioinformatics is a big field. There are highly specialized methods depending on species, tissue, and assay type. CompBioBench publishes a distribution of question types (each benchmark has 99-100 questions). BioMysteryBench has no details on distribution but does mention: 

> In developing this eval, questions were primarily derived from raw or minimally processed DNA or RNA sequencing data since this is where many biological processing pipelines begin (WGS, scRNA-seq, methylation, ChIP-seq, metagenomics, Hi-C), and also included several questions drawn from proteomics and metabolomics.

To compare coverage ofer different types of bioinformatics tasks, I asked Deepseek to map Anthropic's questions onto the domain types that CompBioBench uses[^domain-mapping]:

[^domain-mapping]: Some categories I relabelled to more generally capture the questions between both: Population Genetics → Human Genetics, Structure → Proteomics. Microbiology contains only BioMysteryBench questions; CompBioBench has none.


```{ojs}
benchmarkData = FileAttachment("benchmark-comparison.csv").csv({typed: true})
```

```{ojs}
domainOrder = ["Single-cell", "Epigenomics", "Genomics", "Transcriptomics", "Microbiology", "Human Genetics", "Machine Learning", "Proteomics", "Spatial", "Others"]
styleOrder = ["Metadata Recovery", "Synthetic/Augmented Data", "Routine Analysis", "Retrieval", "Tooling"]
benchmarkOrder = ["CompBioBench", "BioMysteryBench"]
benchmarkColor = ({ domain: benchmarkOrder, range: ["#000000", "#aaaaaa"] })

function benchmarkChart(categoryType, order) {
  const chartData = benchmarkData.filter(d => d.category_type === categoryType)
  return Plot.plot({
    width: 680,
    height: order.length * 34 + 40,
    marginLeft: 200,
    marginRight: 50,
    style: { background: "transparent", fontSize: "13px" },
    fx: { domain: benchmarkOrder, label: null},
    y: { domain: order, label: null, tickSize: 0},
    x: { label: "Number of questions", grid: true, tickSize: 0},
    color: benchmarkColor,
    marks: [
      Plot.barX(chartData, { x: "count", y: "category", fx: "benchmark", fill: "benchmark" }),
      Plot.text(chartData, { x: "count", y: "category", fx: "benchmark", text: d => d.count, dx: 16 }),
      Plot.tip(chartData, Plot.pointerY({
        x: "count",
        y: "category",
        fx: "benchmark",
        title: d => `${d.benchmark}\n${d.category}: ${d.count} questions (${d.pct}%)`
      })),
      Plot.ruleX([0])
    ]
  })
}
```

*BioMysteryBench has only one single cell RNAseq question*! Single cell RNAseq might be one of the most important novel technologies [developed in the last decade](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41573-023-00688-4) [@vandesande2023scrnaseq], and we are at a point where the methods are mature, datasets are plentiful, and so are published peer reviewed well-cited articles. Lacking evaluations on this critical assay type is like evaluating AI on generating accurate physics simulation but saying let's leave out the third dimension. 

What I do like about Anthropic's work is that they more heavily skewed towards bulk RNAseq ("Transcriptomics" in the graphs) - it's sort of the bread & butter of next-generation sequencing assays, because of it's low cost and mature methods, so it's highly relevant. BioMysteryBench also seems to cover a bigger some other data types that are notably lacking in CompBioBench, like proteomics, and microbiology.

Spatial transcriptomics is another data type with minimal coverage: CompBioBench includes only two spatial questions, and BioMysteryBench none. Spatial is becoming an increasingly [important readout in life sciences research and is developing at a rapid pace](https://www.mdpi.com/2073-4409/12/16/2042) [@chen2023spatial]. Many are going to be using AI for spatial analysis, so a more comprehensive benchmark on spatial would be helpful. 

# The reported numbers

Before diving into individual questions, it's worth looking at the results from both publications. 

| | CompBioBench | BioMysteryBench |
|---|---|---|
| **Questions** | 100 | 99 (76 human-solvable, 23 human-difficult)[^99-bmb] |
| **What models are evaluated** | Claude Code Opus 4.6, Codex GPT 5.4, Gemini 3.1 Pro | Claude Mythos Preview, Opus 4.7, Sonnet 4.6 |
| **Best overall** | Codex CLI (GPT-5.4): 83% Accuracy[^CBB-results] | Opus 4.7: 78.9% on human-solvable |
| **Scoring** | Deterministic string matchng | LLM-as-judge with cheat detection |

[^99-bmb]: Currently, BMB is at 90 questions, with 9 questions being removed in a [post-publication review](https://huggingface.co/datasets/Anthropic/BioMysteryBench-full/blob/main/CHANGELOG.md).

[^CBB-results]: CompBioBench compared 4 Claude models, OpenAI's GPT 5.4, and Google's Gemini 3.1 Pro. The results show that the top models from these three companies had similar performance (within a few percentage points). But GPT 5.4 and Gemini 3.1 Pro costing half as much real dollars per task as Anthropic's models. Anthropic's BioMysteryBench only includes their own models in their benchmark. 

# Question difficulty

Moving onto the actual content of these benchmarks, I was curious how hard these questions are. I looked through a bunch of the hardest questions, and here I will just talk about one question from each.

First, Genentech's CompBioBench has difficulty ratings 1-5 (5 is hardest). I could not actually find these difficulty ratings for any of their published questions on huggingface. The only questions with known difficulty are therefore only the ones chosen as "selected examples" in their article's main text.  

Anthropic's BioMysteryBench has a much simpler binary categorization: human-solvable, and human-difficult (or human-unsolvable).

On the most difficult problems (level 4-5 on CompBioBench and "human-unsolvable" on BioMysteryBench), top models got 49-69% accuracy on CompBioBench, but only 19-27% on BioMysteryBench's questions. This suggests that BioMysteryBench has harder questions, which may mean that their benchmark will stay relevant longer, as models get better and better.

# CompBioBench Question Difficulty 4/5

Since I couldn't find a difficult rating for CompBioBench questions, I had to use one of the "selected examples" described in the text. Notably there is one 5/5 difficult problem in their dataset but it's not described in the main text. 

This is a difficulty 4/5 ATACseq question: 

> Q. atac.doublet.q1.bed.gz contains a fragment file from a scATAC-seq sample (hg38). Barcodes with low read counts have been filtered out. Look for doublets. Return the barcode of any one doublet, if any. Respond only with the label of the barcode in the format: “AAATGGAACGTTAAAG-1”, or “None”.

Doublet detection is a standard step in most single cell workflows. The authors note that all model attempts involved applying standard doublet filtering, but the correct answer required using a more advanced doublet detection package called AMULET [@thibodeau2021amulet] [^doublet]. AMULET is able to detect the homotypic doublets, which are when a droplet includes two cells that are the same cell type. Because they are the same cell type, "standard" doublet detection programs which rely on expression patterns cannot detect these. 

[^doublet]: It surprises me that standard scATACseq workflows ignores homotypic doublets because in other assay types like scRNAseq it is standard. (Why is this not already part of the standard workflow?)

The impact of failing to detect homotypic doublets is not discussed. In general leaving a doublet consisting of two cells of the same cell type with the same functional readouts is likely minimally impactful on the analysis. The cases where homotypic doublets might have a large impact are pretty rare, and likely other analyses (like looking at read depth) will inform how much attention is needed to this issue. This question is graded as a simple binary: did the model provide the correct barcode or not. But I would argue that the "wrong" answers were not that wrong. 

I pull this example out because I thought it was one of the few that might be improved or replaced. In general I found most of CompBioBench's questions relevant, instructions are clear, and the evaluations are also clear. I think reliance on synthetic / augmented data is smart, there is not really a way for the model to cheat like in BioMysteryBench, when all the information for the solution must be derived from the data itself. 

# BioMysteryBench Question "Human Unsolvable"

First off, on the term "Human Unsolvable" - the questions are designed by a human expert, they are all solvable questions with self-contained information. What they mean here is that another set of independent human experts could not get the right answer for these questions. I think the term "Human Unsolvable" is not technically correct, and is probably the result of some marketing strategy. They want people to think their models can be smarter than humans. 

> It allows for “superhuman” question generation. By sourcing problems derived from controllable properties of data, BioMysteryBench does not depend on humans being able to solve the problems. In particular, BioMysteryBench contains a handful of problems that—despite having objective, ground-truth solutions—humans found difficult or impossible to solve on their own.

I found the BioMysteryBench data easier to download. Here I worked through one of the unsolvable questions myself.

> This microarray dataset contains expression data from various ovarian and pancreatic cancer biopsies ran on GPL 887 and GPL 4133 platforms, respectively. Based on the expression profile of each sample, assign a sex (male, female, or unknown) to each sample. The final output should be in the format of “Sample; sex” (eg Sample 1; male)

I picked this one because at first glance it's trivially easy and fairly relevant problem: identifying sex of samples can be often helpful in determining sample mix ups, which is an unfortunate but inevitable occurence. 

Identifying sex from any kind of genomic data is a common procedure. It relies on both biological knowledge (how sex differences translate on the genome level), and an understanding of the technology used. There are several parallel paths that one could take to verify sex; stronger defendable answers will involve using multiple lines of evidence.

For RNAseq, or in this case, microarrays, one approach could involve visualizing genes on the sex chromosome such as XIST [^XIST], which will display sex-specific differential expression. 

[^XIST]: a phenomenon where females downregulate X-chromosome derived gene products, as a result of having one more X chromosome than males.

However, the problem is complicated by: multiple tissues, multiple platforms, and cancerous signatures.

Even though gene expression sex differences are large, they might not be surfaced unless accounting for platform/batch and tissue effects. To be safe, we can start by identifying tissue.

The question gives a big hint - it implies one set of tissue samples were measured on one array (ovarian = GPL887), and the other tissues on another (pancreatic = GPL4133). We can see this clearly in that samples 1-6 have non-missing values for a large number of probes, that are not captured on the other. 

The other big piece of information in this question is that it tells you that one set of samples is ovarian. Ovaries is a female reproductive organ. Meaning if you identify which samples are ovarian, then you know the sex of these samples. So identifying tissue identity gives you half the answer already.

In conclusion, my general plan for solving this question:

Identify platform → determines tissue → ovary samples = female, remaining pancreatic samples determine sex by gene expression.

## Identify platform

So first we can map which probe sets correspond to which array, and that will tell us which set of samples are ovarian and which are pancreatic (if the question is correct).

::: {.prompt data-model="deepseek-flash"}
Download and compare the probesets for GPL887 and GPL4133 microarrays. Based on the systematic missing values by probeset for some samples of the Cancers.csv, determine the platform for each sample. Return a data frame that has sample id in one column, and platform (GPL887 vs GPL4133) in another column. Also print the number of probes in both platforms, and the intersection in both.
:::

```{python}
import gzip
import io
import os
import urllib.request

import pandas as pd
from IPython.display import HTML, display

expr = pd.read_csv("Cancers.csv", index_col=0)


def load_platform_table(gpl):
    cache = f"{gpl}_probes.csv"
    if os.path.exists(cache):
        return pd.read_csv(cache, low_memory=False)
    bucket = "GPLnnn" if int(gpl[3:]) < 1000 else f"GPL{gpl[3]}nnn"
    url = f"https://ftp.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/geo/platforms/{bucket}/{gpl}/annot/{gpl}.annot.gz"
    with urllib.request.urlopen(url, timeout=60) as r:
        raw = gzip.decompress(r.read()).decode("utf-8", errors="replace")
    lines = raw.splitlines()
    start = lines.index("!platform_table_begin") + 1
    end = lines.index("!platform_table_end")
    table = pd.read_csv(
        io.StringIO("\n".join(lines[start:end])),
        sep="\t",
        low_memory=False,
        usecols=["ID", "GenBank Accession", "Platform_SPOTID"],
    )
    table.to_csv(cache, index=False)
    return table


gpl887 = load_platform_table("GPL887")
gpl4133 = load_platform_table("GPL4133")

acc887 = set(gpl887["GenBank Accession"].dropna())
acc4133 = set(gpl4133["GenBank Accession"].dropna())

display(
    HTML(
        f"<p>The microarray platform GPL887 has {len(acc887)} features. "
        f"GPL4133 has {len(acc4133)} features. "
        f"The intersection between the two platforms is {len(acc887 & acc4133)} features.</p>"
    )
)

# Cancers.csv column names mix GenBank accessions with Agilent SPOTIDs
# (e.g. "A_24_P704878"), so match on both when identifying which physical
# platform a probe belongs to.
ref887 = acc887 | set(gpl887["Platform_SPOTID"].dropna())
ref4133 = acc4133 | set(gpl4133["Platform_SPOTID"].dropna())

# Don't assume which of the two sample groups is which platform — assign by
# matching each group's uniquely-measured probes (present for that group,
# missing for the other) against each platform's real probe list.
group_masks = [expr.index.isin(range(1, 7)), ~expr.index.isin(range(1, 7))]
group_platform = {}
for mask in group_masks:
    other = ~mask
    private = set(expr.loc[mask].dropna(axis=1).columns) - set(
        expr.loc[other].dropna(axis=1).columns
    )
    votes = {"GPL887": len(private & ref887), "GPL4133": len(private & ref4133)}
    winner = max(votes, key=votes.get)
    for s in expr.index[mask]:
        group_platform[s] = winner

sample_platform = pd.DataFrame(
    {
        "sample": expr.index,
        "missing_probes": expr.isna().sum(axis=1).values,
        "platform": [group_platform[s] for s in expr.index],
    }
)

# For each sample and each platform, what fraction of that platform's
# EXCLUSIVE probe set (accessions/spotids on that chip only, not shared
# with the other platform's design) is non-missing for this sample.
# Probes common to both platforms are excluded here — they're non-missing
# regardless of which platform a sample ran on, so including them dilutes
# the signal instead of separating it.
platform_refs = {"GPL887": ref887 - ref4133, "GPL4133": ref4133 - ref887}
rows = []
for platform, ref in platform_refs.items():
    cols = [c for c in ref if c in expr.columns]
    pct_non_missing = expr[cols].notna().sum(axis=1) / len(cols) * 100
    for s, pct in zip(expr.index, pct_non_missing.values):
        rows.append({"sample": s, "platform": platform, "pct_non_missing": pct})
platform_membership = pd.DataFrame(rows)
ojs_define(platformMembership=platform_membership.to_dict(orient="records"))
```

```{ojs}
platformOrder = ["GPL887", "GPL4133"]
sampleDomain = platformMembership.map(d => d.sample).filter((s, i, a) => a.indexOf(s) === i).sort((a, b) => a - b)

platformMembershipLong = platformMembership.flatMap(d => [
  { sample: d.sample, platform: d.platform, metric: "non-missing", value: d.pct_non_missing },
  { sample: d.sample, platform: d.platform, metric: "missing", value: 100 - d.pct_non_missing }
])

baseFont = 9
axisTitleFont = baseFont * 1.3
facetTitleFont = baseFont * 1.5

platformMembershipPlot = Plot.plot({
  width: 700,
  height: 480,
  marginLeft: 30,
  style: { background: "transparent", fontSize: `${baseFont}px` },
  fx: { domain: platformOrder, axis: null },
  y: { domain: sampleDomain, padding: 0, label: null },
  x: { domain: [0, 100], label: null },
  color: {
    domain: ["non-missing", "missing"],
    range: ["#000000", "#888888"],
    legend: true
  },
  marks: [
    Plot.axisFx({ fontSize: facetTitleFont, label: null }),
    Plot.axisY({ ticks: [1, 7, 10, 20, 30, 40, 49], tickSize: 0, fontSize: baseFont, label: null }),
    Plot.axisX({ tickSize: 0, fontSize: baseFont, label: null }),
    Plot.ruleX([0, 100], { stroke: "#999" }),
    Plot.barX(platformMembershipLong, {
      x: "value",
      y: "sample",
      fx: "platform",
      fill: "metric",
      insetTop: 0,
      insetBottom: 0,
      strokeWidth: 0,
      title: d => `${d.sample} · ${d.platform}\n${d.metric}: ${d.value.toFixed(1)}%`
    })
  ]
})

html`<div style="font-size:${axisTitleFont}px; margin-bottom:0.25rem;"><strong>y:</strong> Sample &nbsp; <strong>x:</strong> % of platform's probeset</div>${platformMembershipPlot}`
```


Based on probe coverage across the two microarray platforms:

- samples 1-6 are GPL4133 and are pancreatic
- remaining samples 7-49 are GPL887 and ovarian, and therefore female

## Sex'ing  pancreatic cancer samples


Now we can turn our effort towards determining the sex of the pancreatic cancer samples 1-6.

Here we can determine sex of these samples based on the expression patterns of good old [XIST](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/XIST), a transcript that is highly expressed in females and not expressed in males. To be extra sure, we can also include a y-chromosome gene RPS4Y1 (expected expressed in males, not in females). To be *extra extra* sure, we can include a larger panel of X-chromosome genes (with PCA + clustering).


::: {.prompt data-model="deepseek-flash"}
Subset to samples 1-6 (pancreatic cancer). Generate three graphs, 1. y-axis samples, x-axis XIST expression, barchart. 2. same as graph 1, but x-axis is RPS4Y1 expression. 3. PCA on samples using the top 100 variable XY probes. Each point is a sample. 
:::


```{python}
import os

import pandas as pd
from sklearn.decomposition import PCA
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler

expr6 = pd.read_csv("Cancers.csv", index_col=0).loc[list(range(1, 7))]
anno = pd.read_csv("refseq_to_symbol_map.csv")
chr_map = dict(pd.read_csv("chr_map.csv").values.tolist()) if os.path.exists("chr_map.csv") else {}
anno["chr"] = anno["REFSEQ"].map(chr_map)
xy = anno[anno["chr"].isin(["X", "Y"])]

xist_probe = anno.loc[anno["SYMBOL"] == "XIST", "REFSEQ"].iloc[0]
rps4y1_probe = "NM_001008"

subset_a_markers = pd.DataFrame(
    {
        "sample": expr6.index,
        "XIST": expr6[xist_probe].values,
        "RPS4Y1": expr6[rps4y1_probe].values,
    }
)
ojs_define(subsetAMarkers=subset_a_markers.to_dict(orient="records"))

# XY probes restricted to just these 6 samples (all on the same platform,
# so no cross-platform missingness to worry about) — this is the full
# platform-specific XY probeset for this subset, not the smaller
# cross-platform-intersected one used elsewhere in this post.
xy_cols = [c for c in xy["REFSEQ"] if c in expr6.columns]
xy_genes = expr6[xy_cols].dropna(axis=1)
xy_variance = xy_genes.var(axis=0).sort_values(ascending=False)

# With only 6 samples, a flat top-100-by-rank cutoff can pad the PCA input
# with probes whose "top" variance is really just noise. Instead, only keep
# probes in the top 10% by variance across the full XY candidate pool —
# this can (and does) return fewer than 100 probes.
variance_floor = xy_variance.quantile(0.90)
selected_xy = xy_variance[xy_variance >= variance_floor].index

top_xy = xy_genes[selected_xy]
X6 = StandardScaler().fit_transform(top_xy)
pcs6 = PCA(n_components=2, random_state=0).fit_transform(X6)

subset_a_xy_pca = pd.DataFrame({"sample": expr6.index, "pc1": pcs6[:, 0], "pc2": pcs6[:, 1]})
ojs_define(subsetAXyPca=subset_a_xy_pca.to_dict(orient="records"))
```

```{ojs}
  height: 220,
  style: { background: "transparent", fontSize: "11px" },
  x: { label: "PC1", tickSize: 0},
  y: { label: "PC2", tickSize: 0},
  marks: [
    Plot.dot(subsetAXyPca, {
      x: "pc1",
      y: "pc2",
      r: 5,
      fill: "#616161",
      title: d => `Sample ${d.sample}\nPC1: ${d.pc1.toFixed(2)}, PC2: ${d.pc2.toFixed(2)}`
    }),
    Plot.ruleX([0]),
    Plot.ruleY([0])
  ]
})

html`<div style="display:flex; flex-wrap:wrap; justify-content:center; gap:1.5rem; align-items:flex-start;">
  <div><div style="font-weight:600; margin-bottom:0.25rem;">XIST expression</div>${subsetABarChart("XIST")}</div>
  <div><div style="font-weight:600; margin-bottom:0.25rem;">RPS4Y1 expression</div>${subsetABarChart("RPS4Y1")}</div>
  <div><div style="font-weight:600; margin-bottom:0.25rem;">PCA, top 100 variable XY probes</div>${subsetAPcaScatter}</div>
</div>`
```


Based on XIST and RPS4Y1 expression, samples 2-3 are likely females, and samples 1, 4, 5, 6 are males. However, the PCA on all XY genes do not separate samples 2/3 from the rest. Cancer is an extremely abnormal process, that might be associated with gene expression changes obscuring the expression of sex-specific genes [^cancer-sex].

[^cancer-sex]: In fact, XIST is expressed in 4% of male cancer samples. See [figure 1G, pancreatic cancer expression of XIST in males vs females](https://www.cell.com/cell-systems/fulltext/S2405-4712(22)00403-3?_returnURL=https%3A%2F%2Flinkinghub.elsevier.com%2Fretrieve%2Fpii%2FS2405471222004033%3Fshowall%3Dtrue) [@sadagopan2022xist].


::: {.prompt data-model="deepseek-flash"}
Generate a plot that shows the a density function of Y chromosome transcript expression - 1 density line for each sample, and color samples 2 and 3 a different color from the rest.

```{python}
import numpy as np
from scipy.stats import gaussian_kde

# Density of Y-chromosome transcript expression, one curve per sample.
y_cols = [c for c in xy[xy["chr"] == "Y"]["REFSEQ"] if c in expr6.columns]
y_genes = expr6[y_cols].dropna(axis=1)

grid = np.linspace(y_genes.values.min() - 1, y_genes.values.max() + 1, 200)
density_rows = []
for sample, row in y_genes.iterrows():
    kde = gaussian_kde(row.values)
    for x, d in zip(grid, kde(grid)):
        density_rows.append({"sample": sample, "x": x, "density": d})

y_density = pd.DataFrame(density_rows)
ojs_define(subsetAYDensity=y_density.to_dict(orient="records"))
```

Y-chromosome transcripts are specific to males. The density plot shows that samples 2 and 3 have mostly background-level signal at Y-chromsome transcripts, indicating that these samples are likely female. They appear distinct from samples 1, 4-6, which have a "flatter" distribution, with more Y- transcripts having above-background levels of expression. 

This analysis finalizes our answers. In the below table, I show every sample in this dataset, a column corresponding to each analysis, and final classification ("My Call"). I then added Anthropic's answer, and another column indicating if I got the answer right for each sample (I didn't, let's see why).

::: {.prompt data-model="deepseek-flash"}

Generate a heatmap that shows male/female based on my analysis (platform, tissue, marker analysis), annotate with anthropics answer. Calculate a final accuracy (% correct).

:::

```{python}
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

sample_platform_lookup = sample_platform.set_index("sample")["platform"]
sex_answer = pd.read_csv("sex_answer.csv")
platform_to_tissue = {"GPL4133": "pancreatic", "GPL887": "ovarian"}

final_calls = pd.DataFrame({"sample": expr.index})
final_calls["platform"] = final_calls["sample"].map(sample_platform_lookup)
final_calls["tissue"] = final_calls["platform"].map(platform_to_tissue)
final_calls["XIST"] = expr[xist_probe].values  # only measured on GPL4133 (samples 1-6)
final_calls["RPS4Y1"] = expr[rps4y1_probe].values

# Pancreatic samples: XIST vs RPS4Y1 (both real signal on GPL4133).
# Ovarian samples: no working sex marker on GPL887 with what's been
# validated so far (RPS4Y1 is flat noise there, std ~0.27 vs ~4.9 on
# GPL4133), so fall back on tissue-of-origin — ovarian cancer occurs
# in genetically female patients.
final_calls["my_call"] = np.where(
    final_calls["tissue"] == "ovarian",
    "female",
    np.where(final_calls["XIST"] > final_calls["RPS4Y1"], "female", "male"),
)
final_calls = final_calls.merge(sex_answer[["sample", "anthropic"]], on="sample")
final_calls["match"] = np.where(final_calls["my_call"] == final_calls["anthropic"], "match", "no match")

# XIST is genuinely missing (NaN) for all ovarian samples. pandas keeps
# that as a float NaN, which serializes to a bare, unquoted `NaN` token —
# invalid JSON that breaks JSON.parse() in the browser. Swap NaN for None
# (-> JSON null) before handing this to ojs_define.
final_calls_json = final_calls.astype(object).where(final_calls.notna(), None).to_dict(orient="records")
ojs_define(subsetAFinalCalls=final_calls_json)


def accuracy_row(label, subset):
    correct = int((subset["match"] == "match").sum())
    n = len(subset)
    return {"label": label, "correct": correct, "n": n, "pct": round(100 * correct / n, 1)}


accuracy_cards = pd.DataFrame(
    [
        accuracy_row("Overall", final_calls),
        accuracy_row("Pancreatic", final_calls[final_calls["tissue"] == "pancreatic"]),
        accuracy_row("Ovarian", final_calls[final_calls["tissue"] == "ovarian"]),
    ]
)
ojs_define(subsetAAccuracyCards=accuracy_cards.to_dict(orient="records"))
```

```{ojs}
// Platform/tissue/XIST/RPS4Y1 stay monotone gray. My call/Anthropic use a
// low-saturation pink/blue pair — enough to read at a glance without being
// loud. Match is plain black/white, high contrast, the one column that
// should jump out over everything else.
grayShades = ({
  platform: { GPL4133: "#dddddd", GPL887: "#f5f5f5" },
  tissue: { pancreatic: "#dddddd", ovarian: "#f5f5f5" }
})
sexColors = ({ male: "#dbe6f2", female: "#f3dde3", unknown: "#eeeeee" })
matchColors = ({ match: "#000000", "no match": "#ffffff" })

xistScale = d3.scaleSequential(d3.interpolateGreys).domain(d3.extent(subsetAFinalCalls, d => d.XIST))
rps4y1Scale = d3.scaleSequential(d3.interpolateGreys).domain(d3.extent(subsetAFinalCalls, d => d.RPS4Y1))

function textColorFor(bg) {
  return d3.lab(bg).l < 55 ? "white" : "black"
}

function finalCallsHeatmap() {
  const columns = [
    { key: "platform", label: "Platform", colors: grayShades.platform, group: "My analysis" },
    { key: "tissue", label: "Tissue", colors: grayShades.tissue, group: "My analysis" },
    { key: "XIST", label: "XIST", scale: xistScale, group: "My analysis" },
    { key: "RPS4Y1", label: "RPS4Y1", scale: rps4y1Scale, group: "My analysis" },
    { key: "my_call", label: "My call", colors: sexColors, group: "My analysis" },
    { key: "anthropic", label: "Anthropic", colors: sexColors, group: null },
    { key: "match", label: "Match", colors: matchColors, group: null }
  ]

  const table = document.createElement("table")
  table.style.cssText = "border-collapse: collapse; font-size: 9px;"

  const groupRow = document.createElement("tr")
  groupRow.appendChild(document.createElement("th"))
  let i = 0
  while (i < columns.length) {
    const group = columns[i].group
    let span = 1
    while (i + span < columns.length && columns[i + span].group === group && group != null) span++
    const th = document.createElement("th")
    th.textContent = group ?? ""
    th.colSpan = group ? span : 1
    // Border only under the actual grouped columns, so the group's real
    // span is visible instead of one line running under the whole table.
    const border = group ? "border-bottom:1px solid #999;" : ""
    th.style.cssText = `padding:1.8px 6px; font-weight:600; text-align:center; ${border}`
    groupRow.appendChild(th)
    i += group ? span : 1
  }
  table.appendChild(groupRow)

  const headerRow = document.createElement("tr")
  headerRow.appendChild(document.createElement("th"))
  for (const col of columns) {
    const th = document.createElement("th")
    th.textContent = col.label
    th.style.cssText = "padding:1.8px 6px; font-weight:600; text-align:center;"
    headerRow.appendChild(th)
  }
  table.appendChild(headerRow)

  for (const d of subsetAFinalCalls) {
    const tr = document.createElement("tr")
    const sampleTd = document.createElement("td")
    sampleTd.textContent = d.sample
    sampleTd.style.cssText = "padding:0.9px 6px; font-weight:600;"
    tr.appendChild(sampleTd)
    for (const col of columns) {
      const value = d[col.key]
      const td = document.createElement("td")
      let bg, text
      if (col.scale) {
        bg = value == null || Number.isNaN(value) ? "#f5f5f5" : col.scale(value)
        text = value == null || Number.isNaN(value) ? "–" : value.toFixed(1)
      } else {
        bg = col.colors[String(value)] ?? "#f5f5f5"
        text = String(value)
      }
      td.textContent = text
      td.title = `Sample ${d.sample} · ${col.label}: ${text}`
      td.style.cssText = `padding:0.9px 6px; text-align:center; background:${bg}; color:${textColorFor(bg)};`
      tr.appendChild(td)
    }
    table.appendChild(tr)
  }
  return table
}

function accuracyCard(d) {
  const box = document.createElement("div")
  box.style.cssText = "border:1px solid black; padding:0.5rem 0.75rem; font-family:monospace; font-size:13.8px; min-width:180px;"
  const label = document.createElement("div")
  label.style.cssText = "font-weight:600; margin-bottom:0.25rem;"
  label.textContent = d.label
  const value = document.createElement("div")
  value.textContent = `Accuracy = ${d.correct}/${d.n} (${d.pct}%)`
  box.append(label, value)
  return box
}

html`<div style="display:flex; flex-direction:column; align-items:center;">
${finalCallsHeatmap()}
<div style="display:flex; flex-wrap:wrap; justify-content:center; gap:0.75rem; margin-top:1rem;">
  ${subsetAAccuracyCards.map(accuracyCard)}
</div>
</div>`
```

# Several wrong answers in BioMysteryBench

The overall accuracy of my classification was 46.9%, worst than random guessing. But in this section let me convince you that I'm right, the answer itself is broken:

1. The answer contains several samples that whose sex is "unknown"

This is problematic for two reasons:

- it suggests that the sex is unverifiable from the provided data. While confounding tissue and technical artifacts may indeed obscure the sex-specific patterns that could be used to determine this answer, it's highly arguable that sex can still be determined with a reasonable level of confidence, especially given that whole transcriptome profiles were provided
- having an "unknown" category as part of the answer, suggests that the task involves providing some level of "confidence" in identifying the label, and choosing an appropriate threshold to call samples as having too low-confidence. How do we, or the models know what a level of "reasonable confidence" is? In practice these kind of thresholds depend entirely on outside context (e.g. the impact of a false negative or false positive), here no context is provided to inform the level of thresholding.

2. The answer itself states that ovarian samples were run on one array. Males don't have ovaries, females do. Instead the answer suggests that even after figuring which samples are ovarian, some of these are actually male samples, or have unknown sex. 

Obviously, the question-answer is a total dud. It should be retracted. I noticed that since publication BioMysteryBench now has 90/99 of the original questions. If we look at the reasons cited for the removal of 9 questions we can see a troubling pattern:

- *hb011 Answer key wrong*
- *hb014 Answer key contradicted by every expert and model rerun*
- *hb040 Infeasible*

It goes on. An additional update modified 24 questions for phrasing and format.

The number of questions that were in the unsolvable set that have been removed are 7, meaning only 10/17 remain. If we recompute (via napkin math) the accuracy to exclude those questions that were flawed, that means that the performance is likely closer to 50-80%. And I just found another question that is broken. How many more questions in BioMysteryBench are flawed? 

It's important to note that there is extensive quality control that Anthropic claims in task creation. This means that a significant percentage of the final questions made it through their quality control process (>10% questions are flawed, >25% needed modification). That is deeply concerning and calls into question the integrity of their benchmark, and the results described.

# Conclusions

It's difficult to create good benchmarks. There's no standard recipe, and every benchmark has a different approach. The ones described in this post had some commonalities in their goals and approaches: the teams tried to create tasks with verifiable ground truth answers, but the execution had some big differences.

Genentech's CompBioBench is high quality and how they published it was highly transparent and reproducible. BioMysteryBench, unfortunately, feels clumsily put together. There are too many errors. The work feels sloppy. 

Despite these differences still, I think they converge on the overall message, that LLMs are indeed highly capable at performing advanced bioinformatics tasks. Using LLMs though, is a skill in itself. Look at the prompts in these questions and it's clear that only an experienced domain expert can generate such specific instructions, and also be in a position to review and check a model's output. LLMs are a multiplier, they require a skilled hand to be used effectively.

I think that LLMs are not necessarily replacing us scientists. There's too much contextual information that can make or break an analysis. But LLMs are certainly making bioinformatics more accessible. That's generally a good thing, but there are also new challenges that brings. If LLMs let more people run these analyses without the years of training that used to be a prerequisite, fewer people will be in a position to catch it when the model is wrong.
